newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French court rules against Renault closure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French court rules against Renault closure.

text.p: A French court on Friday barred automaker Renault from carrying out a procedure for closing its Vilvoorde plant in Belgium until it fulfilled legal obligations to consult its European works council.
Renault quickly said it would appeal the judgment and added that it "awaits the result of this appeal with confidence".

Despite a spate of court challenges and angry protests by Renault workers across Europe, the company has so far given no indication that it could change its mind about the assembly plant's eventual shutdown.

Earlier on Friday Renault said it would appeal against a Belgian court ruling that it had violated Belgium's labour laws with the February 27 announcement of its plan to shut down the Belgian plant, threatening 3,100 jobs.
It said it believed it had fully complied with Belgian law in announcing the closure but would now take up the consultation procedures deemed necessary by the Belgian court.
It said "these procedural elements" did not alter the fact that Renault needed to close the plant for economic reasons.
The Belgian court's decision, issued on Thursday, "does not change Renault's decision to stop ordering vehicles from Renault Industrie Belgique on July 31, 1997," Renault said.

In the French ruling, the court in the Paris suburb of Nanterre said Renault had failed to respect its duty to inform and consult the works council before announcing its intention to shut down the Vilvoorde plant.

It said advance consultations were required as the decision concerned Renault's "strategic orientation and was a major change in a European subsidary that would have repercussions at the European level."

The court said it was barring Renault from pursuing, "even through subsidiaries, the closing procedure for the Vilvoorde plant until it has fulfilled its obligation to inform and consult its European works council".
It was not immediately clear what impact the French ruling would have on Renault's plans.
But the Communist-led CGT union and the more moderate CFDT hailed the French and Belgian judgments and vowed to press ahead with their struggle to keep the plant open.

Angry French, Belgian and Spanish Renault unions had urged work stoppages on Friday in protest at the plant closure as well as Renault plans to cut nearly 2,800 jobs in France and reorganise its dealer network.
In Brussels, Belgian police turned water cannon on some irate workers as an estimated 1,000 Renault employees marched in protest through the centre of the city.

Police acted after some of the workers threw eggs, stones and firecrackers at officers in riot gear and tried to break through a barbed wire barricade in front of the offices of the Flemish regional government.

A spokesman for the Flemish government told them there was little that Flanders, where the doomed plant is located, could do. Any action against French companies might only jeopardise more jobs, the spokesman said.
There were no reports of serious injuries or arrests.

Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer, sticking to his hard line, said in an interview published on Friday in the French daily Liberation that the carmaker might close the Vilvoorde plant earlier than the end of July if workers did not resume production there.

Vilvoorde workers have been occupying the factory, holding billions of francs worth of finished cars hostage, since the closure announcement and have been joined in protests by colleagues from Renault plants in France and Spain.
